extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, agency staff, regulators, and stakeholders interested in rulemaking and generative AI
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analysis on how generative AI intersects with the U.S. notice-and-comment rulemaking process, covering effects on public comments, agency workflows, and possible agency responses and safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments should supply substantive and technical information
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws governing regulatory decisions generally do not call upon, or allow, the agencies to factor in public opinion; rather, agencies seek substantive and technical information from public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments that merely express up-or-down sentiment are less useful; effective comments explain technical data, factual evidence, or legal reasoning that bear on the agency's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating comment counts as a proxy for public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of comments received is not a reliable proxy for general public opinion because submissions are not a representative sample of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should not infer broad public sentiment from raw comment volume; focus instead on the substance and relevance of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and manage mass (identical/near-duplicate) comment campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass comments are 'identical and near-duplicate comments' often sponsored by organizations and submitted by group members and supporters to government agencies in response to proposed rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies already group comments based on textual similarity to meet their legal obligation to consider and respond to significant comments; they should continue and refine these methods to detect sponsored or coordinated campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for generative AI to produce more varied but potentially misleading mass comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining generative AI with mass comment campaigns could lead to mass comments that look less duplicative in nature, making detection and analysis harder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should anticipate increased workload from more differentiated but potentially low-quality or misleading submissions and consider resource and tooling adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not categorically discount comments authored with AI; treat submissions as from persons
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrative Procedure Act only requires that the commenter is a 'person,' and a person could have submitted the comment, no matter who or what drafted it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should avoid blanket policies that dismiss AI-assisted comments; instead, evaluate comments on their factual and legal merits while noting provenance where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify factual assertions in comments rather than accepting them at face value
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency staff work to substantiate the information provided by public comments rather than accepting them at face value; this helps protect rulemaking integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because generative AI can produce plausible but fabricated 'facts' (hallucinations), agencies should continue and perhaps strengthen fact-checking and corroboration practices before relying on comment claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical safeguards on submission platforms to limit automated abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov already implements several techniques to manage large volumes of comments, including a Google CAPTCHA, an authenticated API with terms of service, and throttling limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain or strengthen measures such as CAPTCHA to block automated web submissions, authenticated API keys with revocation ability, and throttling (currently constrained to 50 per minute or 500 per hour) to inhibit abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group similar comments and respond to all significant points
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have access to language processing tools that allow them to group comments based on similarity of their text; this helps agencies meet their burden under the law to consider and respond to all significant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continue using clustering and categorization tools to identify recurring substantive issues and ensure response to material points rather than counting individual near-duplicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generative AI to assist with summarizing, classifying, and drafting responses—only with human expert oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: LLMs can help regulators summarize comments, classify feedback based on predefined categories, and cluster information by similarity, but are most useful when combined with subject-matter expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt workflows where AI produces drafts or analyses that are then verified, corrected, and supplemented by agency staff with topic knowledge before publication (e.g., Federal Register responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: If agencies fine-tune or customize LLMs, make additional training materials public
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency customizes an LLM—e.g., by fine-tuning OpenAI's GPT 3.5—then it will know the additional training materials used (and should make those public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure transparency about the datasets and materials used to train or fine-tune models for rulemaking tasks to allow public scrutiny of potential biases or conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overreliance on contractors or automated tools for inherently governmental functions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is concern about whether drafting rules should be considered an 'inherently governmental function' that is off-limits to contractors; overreliance can introduce conflicts of interest and other risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether use of contractors or LLMs for drafting or core decision work creates conflicts or bias, and maintain human governmental accountability for rule content and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider enhanced oversight and resource planning to balance openness and workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Balancing a notice-and-comment process that is open to all with limited agency resources to consider a large volume of information may require enhanced executive branch and congressional oversight of agency rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for potential spikes in comment volume from AI-assisted submissions by allocating resources, improving tooling, and considering policy changes to manage workload while preserving meaningful public input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful that public comments can be used as training data and may influence model outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments on rules are available on Regulations.gov going back many years, making them a rich source of training data; LLMs trained on such data may reproduce patterns or biases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agencies or others use public comments as training material, consider the implications for bias, representativeness, and the potential feedback loop between comments and AI outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal prohibition on knowingly submitting materially false statements (18 U.S.C. § 1001)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations.gov warns that '[i]t is a violation of federal law to knowingly and willfully make a materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or representation . . . including through comments submitted on Regulations.gov.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complainants should be aware that knowingly submitting fraudulent factual claims may violate federal law, even though prosecution appears rare; agencies should consider legal remedies where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a pooling equilibrium where agencies assume comments may be fake and discount them wholesale
rubrics_metrics.description: Generative AI could reduce the costs of producing 'malattributed' comments and lead to a pooling equilibrium where agencies can no longer meaningfully distinguish between valid and malicious comments, causing them to discount all comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should resist policies that discount public input wholesale; instead, rely on reasoned case-by-case evaluation, corroboration, and legal constraints under the APA to preserve meaningful participation.
